title: Man shot dead by London police faced charges of assaulting Sarnia cops
subtitle: A Sarnia tennis pro fatally shot by London police in a downtown alley last week faced charges of assaulting and obstructing Sarnia police officers.
article: A Sarnia tennis pro fatally shot by London police in a downtown alley last week had recently faced charges of assaulting and obstructing Sarnia police officers, a court heard Tuesday.
Those five charges against Justin Bourassa, 29, were formally withdrawn Tuesday - the same day friends and family held a memorial for him - in a Sarnia courtroom.
"Unfortunately, Mr. Bourassa is now deceased," assistant Crown attorney Aniko Coughlan said during the brief hearing.

The longtime Sarnia Tennis Club member, competitive player and instructor was killed in an encounter with London police last Thursday that's now being probed by the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), Ontario's police watchdog.

Bourassa faced two counts of assaulting a peace officer and one count of obstructing a peace officer stemming from an alleged incident Feb. 19, 2021. Two other counts of assaulting a peace officer are related to allegations from Aug. 27, 2021 the court heard.

Justice of the peace Helen Gale withdrew the charges during the brief hearing, attended by Bourassa's lawyer, Sarnia-area criminal defence attorney Sarah Donohue, who later declined to comment on the case.
A Sarnia police spokesperson declined to provide information about the charges against Bourassa, citing the SIU probe.

On the day Bourassa died, London police were called to a break-in near St. George and Mill streets about 3:45 a.m. An officer saw a man in a nearby Richmond Row alley, where there was "an interaction" and an officer shot the man, the SIU said.
Neither the SIU nor London police have linked Bourassa to the break-in call, and the circumstances leading to the fatal shooting remain unclear.
A tennis pro who also worked as a massage therapist was the man fatally shot by London police in a downtown alley last week, The London Free Press has learned.

Citing a source at the Sarnia Tennis Club, The London Free Press identified Bourassa as the man shot and killed by London police in a story published Tuesday. The SIU later released Bourassa's identity, saying his family had given their consent.
The SIU didn't release his identity Oct. 29 because it said it didn't have the consent of the family then.

Bourassa's death has rattled members of Lambton County's tight-knit tennis community, many of whom were among the 200 people who gathered Tuesday night at the Sarnia Tennis Club for a candlelight vigil.
Notebooks were on site for people to leave messages for his family. Friends have described Bourassa as a gifted athlete with a great sense of humour.

Bourassa, a 2014 graduate of Lambton College's massage therapy program, worked as head tennis pro at the Sarnia club, taught tennis at a city-run summer camp and had his own massage therapy practice, according to his LinkedIn profile.

But Bourassa's certificate to practise massage therapy in Ontario has been inactive since the year began, according to the Ontario College of Massage Therapists, the industry regulator. A college spokesperson said Bourassa's inactive certificate meant he wasn't allowed to practise massage therapy or use the title registered massage therapist.

"While we cannot comment on the specific reason for an RMT (registered massage therapist) to be registered in the inactive class, RMTs with this class of registration typically do not intend to practise massage therapy for a period of time due to reasons such as a parental or educational leave," Angie Brennand said by email.
It's unclear why Bourassa, whose certificate had been active since 2014, allowed his certification to lapse this year.
